# MLOps: machine learning in production {.unnumbered}

> *"Only a small fraction of real-world ML systems is composed of the ML
> code… The required surrounding infrastructure is vast and complex."*
> — D. Sculley et al., 2015 [@sculley2015]

This part corresponds to the seventh course of the master. Parts III and IV
taught how to **build** a model; Parts V and VI how to **package** a program
and give it an **API**. This part is about what happens next: keeping a
model working, for months, in front of real traffic, while data, code and the
world change underneath it. That discipline is called **MLOps** — the
practices that make machine learning systems reproducible, tested, deployed
automatically, observed, and retrained on purpose rather than by accident.

The chapters follow the modules of the course — what MLOps is; isolated
environments and version control for code, data and models; serving a model
over HTTP; testing; containers and deployment; continuous integration and
delivery; monitoring; orchestration — and go beneath each of them. Every
practice comes with the quantity that justifies it: how many examples a
model test needs before its verdict means anything, how large a canary must
be to see a 2-point drop, why the population stability index is a symmetric
Kullback–Leibler divergence, how to estimate the sentiment mix of a stream
**without labels**, how long to wait before an alert fires, when retraining
pays for itself.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this part matters for an AI engineer
Most models that fail in production do not fail with an exception. They keep
answering — with a stale dependency, a feature computed differently than in
training, inputs that have drifted away from anything seen before, or a
world in which the same words now mean something else. Industry surveys of
deployments find the same obstacles again and again: reproducing results,
moving from notebook to service, testing, monitoring [@paleyes2022;
@amershi2019]. The engineering in this part is what turns a model that
worked once into a system that keeps working — and that tells you when it
stops.
:::

## What you will be able to do {.unnumbered}

1. Explain the life cycle of an ML system, the roles around it, the kinds of
   technical debt it accumulates, and assess its maturity with explicit
   rubrics; measure **prediction churn** between model versions
   (@sec-ch-ops-intro).
2. Make a project **reproducible**: pinned and hashed environments, Git as a
   content-addressed store, experiment tracking, a model registry with
   aliases and lineage from data to deployed image (@sec-ch-ops-repro).
3. **Serve** a model with FastAPI: load once, validate inputs, expose
   prediction and health endpoints, return **calibrated** probabilities, and
   size micro-batching with Little's law (@sec-ch-ops-serving).
4. **Test** an ML system: unit, integration and contract tests with pytest,
   linting and formatting with Ruff, behavioural tests of the model, and
   quality tests with a controlled false-failure rate (@sec-ch-ops-testing).
5. **Deploy** it: a lean, deterministic image for the model service, and
   release strategies — rolling, blue/green, shadow, canary — with the sample
   sizes that make a canary meaningful (@sec-ch-ops-deploy).
6. Build **CI/CD** pipelines with GitHub Actions, order their stages, gate
   the promotion of a model with a paired statistical test, and publish an
   image (@sec-ch-ops-cicd).
7. **Monitor** a model service: golden signals and SLOs, Prometheus metrics
   and alerts, Docker Compose stacks, Grafana dashboards; detect **data and
   concept drift** (PSI, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, χ²), estimate **label shift**
   without labels, and detect changes sequentially with CUSUM
   (@sec-ch-ops-monitor).
8. **Orchestrate** the cycle with DAGs: topological order, critical path,
   idempotent tasks, Airflow with returned values, and retraining policies
   with their cost model (@sec-ch-ops-orch).

## Prerequisites {.unnumbered}

From Part I: virtual environments and requirements (@sec-ch-venv,
@sec-requirements), files and JSON (@sec-json), exceptions
(@sec-ch-exceptions). From Parts III and IV: train/test splits and
cross-validation (@sec-cross-validation), leakage (@sec-leakage),
classification metrics (@sec-classification-metrics), the test-set bound
(@thm-test-set-size). From Part V: images, layers and digests, Kubernetes
rollouts (@sec-ch-ctr-containers). From Part VI: HTTP, FastAPI, idempotence,
Little's law, tail latency, token buckets (@sec-ch-api-rest). The
probability used — expectations, the binomial and normal distributions,
hypothesis tests at the level of a first course — is introduced where needed.

## Graded practice {.unnumbered}

Every main section ends with a **Practice** block — **Easy** (by hand),
**Medium** (in code), **Hard** (a small open problem) — each with a collapsed
hint and a separate collapsed solution, with executed code. Unlike Parts V
and VI this course **has a final project**, and the Hard exercises move in
its direction — a sentiment classifier served, tested, packaged, released,
monitored and retrained — on the small local model of the theory chapters,
without solving the project itself.

## Data and models of the theory chapters {.unnumbered}

The theory chapters do not depend on any downloaded model or dataset. They
use **synthetic short posts** generated in code by the part's helper,
[`mlops/opsbook.py`](https://github.com/matteo-zirilli/ai-engineering-handbook/blob/main/mlops/opsbook.py):
each post mentions a product topic, may contain polar words, negations,
emojis or slang, and carries a label 0 = negative, 1 = neutral, 2 = positive
(the encoding of the model used in the project), with 6 % annotation noise.
The generator exposes every kind of change studied in @sec-ch-ops-monitor as
a parameter — class priors (label shift), topics, length, emojis, unseen
slang (covariate shift), words that change polarity (concept shift) — so
that each formula can be checked against a known truth. The model is small
and trains in a fraction of a second: TF-IDF features of words and word
pairs and a multinomial logistic regression (@sec-ch-ml-classification).
No real person's text is used anywhere in the theory chapters.

## Tools and versions {.unnumbered}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
import sys, subprocess
from importlib.metadata import version
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import opsbook as ob

def v(cmd):
    return subprocess.run(cmd, shell=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout.strip()

mlflow_v = v(f"{ob.venv_python('mlflow')} -c 'import mlflow; print(mlflow.__version__)'")
airflow_v = v(f"{ob.venv_python('airflow')} -c 'import airflow; print(airflow.__version__)'")
prom_v = v(f"{ob.tool('prometheus')} --version").split()[2]
am_v = v(f"{ob.tool('alertmanager')} --version").split()[2]
docker_v = v("docker version --format '{{.Server.Version}}'") or "not running"
compose_v = v("docker compose version --short")
print(f"The code of this part was executed with **Python {sys.version.split()[0]}**, "
      f"scikit-learn {version('scikit-learn')}, NumPy {version('numpy')}, SciPy {version('scipy')}, "
      f"pandas {version('pandas')}; **FastAPI {version('fastapi')}**, Pydantic {version('pydantic')}, "
      f"uvicorn {version('uvicorn')}, httpx {version('httpx')}; **pytest {version('pytest')}**, "
      f"**Ruff {version('ruff')}**; prometheus-client {version('prometheus-client')}; "
      f"**MLflow {mlflow_v}** and **Apache Airflow {airflow_v}** (each in its own virtual environment); "
      f"**Prometheus {prom_v}** and **Alertmanager {am_v}**, **actionlint {v(ob.tool('actionlint') + ' --version').splitlines()[0]}** "
      f"and **act {v(ob.tool('act') + ' --version').split()[-1]}** (binaries from their GitHub releases); "
      f"**Docker Engine {docker_v}** with **Compose {compose_v}**. Every output shown was produced by "
      "actually running the code when the book was built.")
```

All services run on the build machine's loopback interface. The build
machine cannot reach Docker Hub or any other image registry, so images are
built from local stand-ins of the official base images, exactly as in
Part V; it cannot download Grafana either, so Grafana's configuration
(data source, dashboard, alert rule) is written, validated and explained,
but not rendered by a running Grafana — Prometheus and Alertmanager, which
can be downloaded, run for real.

## Map of the part {.unnumbered}

| Chapter | Core topics | What the book adds |
|---|---|---|
| @sec-ch-ops-intro | what MLOps is, life cycle, roles, maturity models, tool stack, model hubs and model cards | prediction churn and its bounds, technical debt made concrete, the ML Test Score as a computation, content-pinned downloads |
| @sec-ch-ops-repro | virtual environments, version control, model versioning, registries | what determines a run, floating-point non-associativity, Git objects computed by hand, `git bisect` on a model, MLflow tracking and aliases, lineage by hashes |
| @sec-ch-ops-serving | serving patterns, HTTP APIs for models, FastAPI | load-once cost model, schema validation and health/readiness, calibration (ECE, temperature scaling with proofs), micro-batching and Little's law |
| @sec-ch-ops-testing | why test, kinds of tests, linting and formatting, pytest, testing models | the ML Test Score's categories, fixtures and contracts, formatter idempotence, behavioural tests (invariance, direction), Wilson intervals and test sizing with power |
| @sec-ch-ops-deploy | deployment, containers, Docker images for models | baking vs fetching the model, health checks, rolling/blue-green/shadow/canary, two-proportion sample sizes |
| @sec-ch-ops-cicd | CI/CD, pipeline stages, services, GitHub Actions, continuous delivery | optimal stage order (exchange argument), critical path, actionlint and local runs, McNemar's test as a promotion gate |
| @sec-ch-ops-monitor | what to monitor, data and concept drift, Docker Compose, Grafana, alerts | quantiles from histograms, PSI = Jeffreys divergence, KS + DKW sample sizes, χ², BBSE and EM for label shift, CUSUM, `for:` durations and false alarms |
| @sec-ch-ops-orch | orchestrators, DAGs, Airflow, returned values | Kahn's algorithm proved, span and work bounds, idempotent partitions, the optimal retraining period, feedback loops |

## The project {.unnumbered}

The course ends with a project: take a **pre-trained sentiment classifier
for social-media posts** (a RoBERTa model fine-tuned on tweets, published on
the Hugging Face Hub) and carry it through the whole chain of this part — a
tested FastAPI service, a reproducible environment and a readable history, a
container image, a CI/CD pipeline, metrics with a dashboard and an alert, a
discussion of the drift signals to watch, and an orchestrated cycle of data
collection, evaluation and retraining. The project chapter restates the
requirements in my own words, maps each to the chapters above, and walks
through a complete reference implementation. It is **in preparation**: the
build machine cannot reach the Hugging Face Hub, so the way the model's files
reach the book, and the public dataset with a clear licence used to evaluate
it, are being settled with the author before the chapter is written. Each
theory chapter's "In the project" box already says which of its tools the
project needs.
